title: Real wages falling for past year
full_text:
Jim Chalmers admits the country’s dire productivity and high inflation are eating away at workers’ pay packets after new data showed real wages have been falling for the past year just as public sector wages have outstripped the private sector.
Inflation is running hot at between 3.9 and 4.3 per cent, depending on the use of quarterly or monthly data, while annual nominal wage growth is 3.5 per cent, leaving real wages going backwards by between -0.4 per cent and -0.8 per cent in the year to September.
The latest figures show the government has now presided over more quarters of inflation being ahead of wages than wages being ahead of inflation.
“Real wages are declining not because wages have been too low but because inflation is still too high,” Dr Chalmers said on Wednesday in recognition that inflation had also now been outside the RBA’s preferred target range for 14 out of 18 quarters.
The Treasurer acknowledged that productivity, which is currently going backwards at a rate of -0.2 per cent and has been downgraded by both Treasury and the Reserve Bank this year, was crucial for boosting wage growth.
“We recognise that productivity is the long-term driver of wages growth in our economy,” Dr Chalmers said.
He also took credit for the independent Fair Work Commission’s minimum pay rises this year which economists said were a “key contributor to the rise” in wages. A 4.75 per cent rise in awards wage for the 2027 financial year was reflected in the latest data for the first time. Last year, the awards wage rose 3.5 per cent.
“We’re helping to deliver higher wages for workers because we know this is one of the best ways to help with the cost of living,” Dr Chalmers said.
Without accounting for inflation, wages grew 1.1pc in the September quarter, with public sector wages growing at 1.3 per cent in the quarter, exceeding private sector wage growth of 1 per cent. On an annual basis, public sector wages have now outstripped the private sector for the seventh consecutive quarter. Public-sector wages grew 3.9 per cent, while private-sector grew 3.4 per cent.
Healthcare and social assistance was the largest contributor to overall quarterly growth with wages in healthcare and social assistance growing at 2.6 per cent in the quarter and 4.9 per cent annually, according to the Australian Bureau of Statistics.
The Treasurer said Labor was supporting the wage increases for 2.8 million workers on the National Minimum Wage, with up to 460,000 health, disability and community services workers and 400,000 aged care workers.
Economists said that the combination of labour costs and poor productivity would mean there was still some pressure on the RBA around rate hikes.
NAB economist Michael Hayes said the wage data was only modestly above the RBA’s November forecasts, “but alongside weak productivity growth and more elevated unit labour cost pressure, the data will, at the margin, further feed the RBA’s concern they had been underappreciating the extent of domestic capacity and labour market pressure.” EY chief economist Cherelle Murphy said weak productivity growth meant businesses were hit by higher labour costs, while households were finding their pay packets worth less because of business passing on higher prices.
“While Australia is not experiencing a wage-price spiral, weak productivity growth is translating into relatively strong growth in unit labour costs. This raises the risk that businesses pass on more of their cost increases to consumers,” Ms Murphy said.
“For households, stronger pay packets were eroded by higher prices. Real wages fell again in the quarter, adding to cost-of-living pressures and the challenges facing businesses that serve them. The Reserve Bank is tackling the challenge by aggressively trying to bring inflation down,” she said.
Ms Murphy said that while the nominal wage growth figure was “uncomfortably high for the central bank”, it was “unlikely to prompt any immediate reaction given the economy is now slowing in response to the five interest rate hikes”.
This month the Reserve Bank downgraded its forecast for its preferred measure of wages – the real average earnings per hour. It now expects that measure to fall -0.9 per cent by December this year, down from its previous forecast of a -0.5 per cent contraction, while it now expects 0 per cent growth by June next year, down from its previous forecast of 0.8 per cent growth.
RBA governor Michele Bullock told reporters this month some board members who voted against hiking rates for the fifth time this year cited poor wages growth as a reason to hold off. “I think those looking for a hold were thinking that housing has reacted, the unemployment rate is drifting up, there is no sign of wages growth accelerating,” Ms Bullock said.
Official meeting minutes from the bank’s last rate hike decision noted that wage growth was slowing due to poor productivity levels.
“Wages growth for workers on individual arrangements (which tends to be most responsive to labour market conditions) had slowed. Members discussed the extent to which ongoing weak productivity growth might reconcile trends in the Wage Price Index,” minutes said.
Opposition Treasury spokesman Tim Wilson blamed Labor for “more disturbing data that Australians are having their wages eaten into by inflation”.
“Over the life of the Albanese government, we’ve had a 17 per cent increase in wages, but it’s been eclipsed by an increase of 18.3 per cent (in) inflation,” he said.
The ABS noted that “the main driver of public sector wage growth was pay rises for state government frontline workers covered by enterprise agreements”. The official public service wage bill during the 2026 financial year showed state government costs increased $12.6bn, or 6.6 per cent. The federal government wage costs climbed 7.2 per cent, or $3bn.
